content.one_sentence_role: Uses Hölder’s inequality to turn strong $L^n$ convergence of matrix fields into convergence of their determinant integrals.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $n\geq1$, let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a measure space, and let $\mathcal F$ be any filter on an index set $I$. Let $P_i,Q:\Omega\to\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^n)$, equipped with the operator norm induced by $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ on $\mathbb R^n$. Suppose $Q\in L^n(\mu)$, eventually $P_i\in L^n(\mu)$ along $\mathcal F$, and
$$\|P_i-Q\|_{L^n(\mu)}\longrightarrow0\quad(i\to\mathcal F).$$
Then $\int_\Omega\det P_i\,d\mu\to\int_\Omega\det Q\,d\mu$ along the same filter.
content.assumptions: The dimension is positive. Membership in $L^n$ includes almost-everywhere strong measurability and finite seminorm. The measure need not be finite, and the filter need not be a sequence filter. No pointwise convergence or common pointwise bound is assumed.
content.conclusion: The limiting determinant is integrable, the approximating determinants are eventually integrable, and their integrals converge. In fact their differences converge to zero in $L^1(\mu)$.
content.proof_summary: Apply the determinant difference estimate, then Hölder with exponents $n/(n-1)$ and $n$. The resulting bound contains the factor $\|P_i-Q\|_{L^n}$, which tends to zero; the other factor stays bounded by the triangle inequality. Treat $n=1$ directly.

proof_steps.text:
**Start with the pointwise estimate and integrability.** The determinant bound gives, at every $x$,
$$\begin{aligned}
|\det P_i(x)-\det Q(x)|
&\leq n\bigl(\|P_i(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|Q(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\bigr)^{n-1}
\|P_i(x)-Q(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\end{aligned}$$
For any field $T\in L^n(\mu)$, comparison with the zero operator gives
$$|\det T(x)|\leq n\|T(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^n,\qquad
\int_\Omega n\|T(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^n\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Continuity of determinant supplies measurability, so $\det T$ is integrable. Apply this to $Q$ and, eventually, to $P_i$. Hence the determinant difference is eventually integrable. All following estimates are on this eventual set of indices.

**Take the limit and then subtract the integrals.** Since $\|P_i-Q\|_{L^n(\mu)}\to0$, eventually it is at most $1$. The last bound in Step 3 is then at most
$$n\bigl(1+2\|Q\|_{L^n(\mu)}\bigr)^{n-1}\|P_i-Q\|_{L^n(\mu)}\longrightarrow0.$$
The coefficient is finite because $Q\in L^n(\mu)$. Together with Step 2 this proves $L^1$ convergence for every $n\geq1$. The integrability checked in Step 1 now justifies
$$\begin{aligned}
\left|\int_\Omega\det P_i\,d\mu-\int_\Omega\det Q\,d\mu\right|
&=\left|\int_\Omega(\det P_i-\det Q)\,d\mu\right|\\
&\leq\|\det P_i-\det Q\|_{L^1(\mu)}\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}$$
All eventual statements and limits use the same filter $\mathcal F$; neither finite total measure nor a sequence index was assumed.

content.lean_realization_notes: The supplied convergence predicate records both seminorm convergence and eventual membership; the separate hypothesis on $Q$ is also necessary for the proof. The one-dimensional case is handled directly, without using the undefined exponent $n/(n-1)$ at $n=1$.
